sentences.text: Phorusrhacos stood between 1.4 and 1.9 meters tall and weighed approximately 93 kilograms. Unlike similarly sized relatives like Kelenken and Devincenzia, this animal was more lithe and built for running.
Its skull was laterally compressed, especially when viewed from the front. It possessed short, thick, and broad cervical vertebrae that may have strengthened its neck for powerful strikes.
The etymology of the name is convoluted because the original describer did not explain the origin of the generic or specific names.

The first fossil was discovered in 1887 by Carlos Ameghino in the Santa Cruz Formation of Santa Cruz Province, Argentina. He initially misidentified the fossil as a giant, toothless sloth and placed it in the family Phorusrhacidae.
In 1891, Francisco Moreno correctly identified the specimen as a bird rather than a mammal.
The holotype specimen of P. longissimus is mandible MLP-118.
Phorusrhacos acted as an apex predator in Santacrucian ecosystems, likely hunting ground sloths, notoungulates, and litopterns.
However, it primarily fed on small prey and carrion.
Carlos Ameghino classified Phorusrhacidae within the Ratites, a group of giant birds including ostriches, Aepyornis, and Dinornis.

In 1989, Luis M. Chiappe and Miguel F. Soria appealed to the ICZN to conserve the name Phororhacos and suppress Phorusrhacos. The ICZN Commission rejected the names Phororhacos and Phororhacosidae following a ruling.
Phorusrhacos lived during the Early to Middle Miocene, specifically from the Burdigalian to Serravallian stages.
It inhabited Patagonia, living in forests and grasslands.
The taxonomic history of Phorusrhacos is considered muddled due to fragmentary fossils and a lack of scientific consensus.
Sinclair and Farr suggested that Phorusrhacidae might be a paraphyletic clade, a view later authors did not support.
While Dolgopol de Sáez thought Liornis was related to Brontornis, Alvarenga and Höfling argued in 2003 that it is a synonym of P. longissimus.
Alvarenga and Höfling also argued in 2003 for the continued use of the name Mesembriornis, a view that has received some recognition.
